title: Rollout latency: seasonal p99 triggers and mitigation plan
content:
Summary:

This doc captures an in-progress investigation into a recurring p99 latency spike observed during the last three multi-model rollouts (v3.2 -> v3.3) across production clusters. The p50/p95 numbers are largely stable but p99 worsened significantly during specific windows (peak traffic and a repeat 02:00 UTC cohort). We believe the root cause is an emergent interaction between model variant warm-start behavior, KV-cache miss storms, and transient batching head-of-line blocking when cold-cache traces interleave with hot-cache traffic.

Key observed symptomset (production telemetry snapshots):
- Baseline (pre-rollout): p50=38ms, p95=140ms, p99=480ms
- During affected rollout windows: p50=42ms (+10%), p95=165ms (+18%), p99=1.28s (+167%)
- Affected traces are concentrated in two cohorts: sequence-length > 1024 and requests routed to region-us-west-2 nodes where the newer variant first reached 75% traffic.
- KV cache hit-rate drops from 92% to ~61% for a few minutes after a canary ramp step.

Per-stage median/quantile breakdown (snapshots taken from aggregated trace sampler for affected cohort):
- Tokenize: p50 8ms / p95 12ms / p99 20ms
- Routing & auth: p50 2ms / p95 5ms / p99 10ms
- KV cache lookup (hit path): p50 1ms / p95 3ms / p99 5ms
- KV cache miss (backend fetch + merge): p50 70ms / p95 150ms / p99 520ms
- Batcher wait (head-of-line): p50 4ms / p95 30ms / p99 450ms
- Compute kernels (per-token emit): p50 22ms / p95 40ms / p99 120ms
- Emit/serialize: p50 3ms / p95 8ms / p99 14ms
- Egress/network: p50 2ms / p95 4ms / p99 8ms

Interpretation and how these add up: the p99 tail is dominated by two disjoint but interacting phenomena:
1) KV cache miss storms that trigger expensive backend fetch+rehydration (miss path ~200-520ms depending on seq len), and
2) A small fraction of requests experiences large batcher wait times (150-450ms) when a cold-cache request is routed to a node that had been serving hot traffic: the cold request insertion causes the batcher to stall while the compute node swaps kernel variant / warms quantization tables and commits larger tensors into GPU memory.

Hypotheses considered (rank-ordered):
- H1: Model variant v3.3 changed internal key layout (embedding prefixing) so previously-warm entries no longer match, causing transient cache misses during rollout.
- H2: Kernel selection path for v3.3 triggers a slower fallback kernel on ~3% of sequences when sequence length > 1024 (edge case in our kernel selector). That slower kernel amplifies batcher wait for subsequent requests.
- H3: Autoscaler and placement policy placed new instances without warmed KV caches into hot routing pools during canary steps, increasing effective miss rate.
- H4: Client-side retry/backoff jitter patterns during rollout intensify hot-path re-entries causing brief microbursts (observed 50-200 QPS spikes at cluster ingress).

Quick evidence map against hypotheses:
- H1: Confirmed partial correlation. We inspected the model metadata and found a change to the prefix that affects cache key canonicalization for tokenized prompts that include system messages. Kernel of evidence: when we replayed sampled prompts with v3.2->v3.3 model switching, cache key mismatch spiked.
- H2: Replayed traces on bench hardware and saw a ~3.4x longer kernel path for >1024 sequence in ~2.7% of inputs; stack trace on the kernel selector shows fallback code path taken when layer fused-ops table mismatch occurs.
- H3: Placement logs show new instances joining routing tables with cold caches; however we also saw instances that had been up but still exhibiting cache miss bursts, so placement is a contributor but not sole cause.
- H4: Ingress QPS jitter correlates with the exact windows of spike in one rollout; secondary, less consistent evidence.

Investigations run so far (short checklist):
- Replayed 10k sampled production prompts against v3.3 in bench env (Benji) -> reproduced miss-rate increase when model metadata pref changed.
- Kernel selector trace added to nightly benchmark: identified fallback signature for >1024 sequences (Claire).
- Synthetic canary with warmed cache vs cold canary -> confirmed cold canary causes transient p99 spikes.
- Cross-checked autoscaler and placement logs for rollouts -> found placement windows coincident with spikes.

Proposed short-term mitigations (low-risk, quick):
- Stop the current global ramp and pause at 10% traffic for an additional warmup window (15–30 minutes) while running a cache-warm job that sends representative prompts to new instances (Action: Daniel -> create SERV ticket).
- Add a temporary policy to route 100% of high-seqlen (>1024) traffic to stable instances until kernel selector patch lands. Implement via routing weight override (Action: Aisha).
- Increase batcher prefetch timeout cap slightly to avoid long head-of-line for the small percent of cold requests (from 50ms -> 80ms) while monitoring throughput impact (Action: Claire).

Proposed medium-term fixes (3–6 days):
- Fix cache canonicalization: add backward-compatible normalization layer in cache key generation that maps both prefixes for 48 hours post-rollout. Also add a rolling migration that warms keys. (PR: linked above)
- Patch kernel selector to avoid slow fallback on >1024 sequences and add unit tests that cover the fused-op table mismatch scenario.
- Add rollout playbook change: always perform staged warm-up with a policy that ensures at least one warmed replica per placement zone before crossing 25% ramp threshold.

Longer-term (2+ weeks):
- Improve KV cache telemetry: expose per-replica key-set cardinality and a compact bloom filter snapshot for quick health checks during rollouts.
- Add an auto-warm path that proactively populates cache on new replica startup using a small sampled request corpus (respecting PII/data policy).

Immediate experiments to run (ordered):
1) Controlled canary with warmed cache vs cold canary in us-west-2 at 02:00 UTC to reproduce (owner Benji). Metrics: p99, kv-hit-rate, batcher-wait-quantiles.
2) Kernel-selector A/B on bench nodes for >1024 sequences (owner Claire). Measure compute tail and whether fallback happens.
3) Short synthetic microburst injection to measure head-of-line sensitivity (owner Daniel).

Sample trace excerpts (representative p99):
- trace:abc12345 – SEQ_LEN=1280 – Tokenize 12ms | KV-lookup miss->backend 430ms | Batcher wait 380ms | Compute 110ms | emit 8ms -> total 948ms
- trace:xyz9876 – SEQ_LEN=64 – Tokenize 6ms | KV-lookup hit 1ms | Batcher wait 12ms | Compute 28ms | emit 4ms -> total 51ms

Open questions and unresolved edges:
- Can we safely add a compatible normalization mapping without producing duplicate cache entries that cause inconsistent merges? (need design review)
- Is the kernel fallback triggered by a benign metadata mismatch or by a micro-version difference in compiled operators? If the latter, we need to audit build artifact provenance for that release.
- Will temporarily increasing batcher delay materially impact p95 throughput or cost? We need a controlled experiment.

Action items (short):
- Aisha: enact routing override for high-seqlen traffic (short config change). (Target: today EOD)
- Benji: run warmed vs cold canary experiment and post summarized telemetry (Target: +6h) -> create SERV-3214
- Claire: submit kernel-selector patch PR and bench test (Target: +48h) -> PR #846
- Daniel: create warmup job template and SERV runbook snippet (Target: +24h)

Notes to reviewers: this doc is intentionally conversational and contains early hypotheses. Please add any trace IDs or telemetry slices you think are relevant (use linked Slack thread). If you disagree with short-term mitigations, propose alternatives here before we pause the rollout.

Appendix (raw telemetry pointers):
- p99 spike windows: 2026-02-14 01:58–02:12 UTC, 2026-02-19 02:03–02:27 UTC, 2026-02-23 22:40–22:55 UTC
- Example trace ids for deeper debugging: abc12345, fgh45678, xyz9876
- Bench replay harness used: github.com/redwood-inference/trace-replay/tree/warmup-scripts

End.
